**Retrieval note:** All IEA source URLs returned Cloudflare security-verification pages at time of generation. No verbatim content was extractable from these sources. Source 1 (Eurostat) is the sole span-groundable source in this brief. IEA sources 2–7 are listed for registry tracking and as targets for re-retrieval in the next cycle.

---

**Eurostat next planned update — FACT:**

The Eurostat Electricity Price Statistics article carries a planned update date of 30 October 2026, when H1 2026 non-household price data will be published. *Source: Eurostat, Electricity Price Statistics, data extracted April 2026. https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Electricity_price_statistics

*Operational implication:* The 30 October 2026 Eurostat update is the next anchor point for refreshing EU non-household electricity cost baselines. Workspaces with EU facility investments or energy cost clauses in client contracts should calendar this date for a rate check.

**IEA Electricity 2026 full report:**

*Analytical inference:* The IEA Electricity 2026 report (corroborator URL: https://www.iea.org/reports/electricity-2026/prices) is described as containing current price analysis through 2025. When IEA pages become accessible (Cloudflare block is a transient retrieval issue, not a content withdrawal), this source should be retrieved and span-grounded to confirm or update the cross-regional price differentials. Re-check: next regeneration cycle or when IEA access is confirmed restored.

MONITORING — IEA Electricity 2026 prices page: re-check within 30 days for Cloudflare access restoration. If the 2x US / 1.5x China differential is span-confirmed, it should be promoted to FACT and the cross-regional sections updated accordingly.

**EU ETS Phase 4 tightening (2026–2030):**

*Analytical inference:* EU ETS free allocation for industrial electricity consumers continues to contract under Phase 4 through 2030. Carbon cost pass-through from generators into industrial electricity prices faces upward structural pressure regardless of fuel market direction. The specific magnitude of ETS-linked electricity cost increases requires a dedicated EU ETS Operations Profile brief. This item is flagged as a pending change that could materially shift the EU vs. US and EU vs. China cost comparison currently estimated at 2x and 1.5x respectively.

**EU renewables buildout — moderating pressure:**

*Analytical inference:* Accelerated EU solar and wind deployment (EU Solar Energy Strategy, REPowerEU) is a structural moderating force on wholesale electricity prices. The extent to which wholesale reductions pass through to non-household industrial rates depends on network cost recovery mechanisms, which vary by member state. No sourced forecast of the magnitude or timeline of this moderation was available from the accessible source blocks.

---

**On-site solar and BESS at EU logistics facilities:**

*Analytical inference:* The 3.4x spread in non-household electricity prices across EU member states (Finland €0.0748/kWh vs. Ireland €0.2552/kWh in H2 2025) means the payback threshold for on-site solar and battery energy storage systems varies significantly by country. At German or Irish cost levels, the financial case for behind-the-meter generation is materially stronger than at Finnish or Swedish levels. Workspaces evaluating European consolidation hub investments should run on-site generation feasibility against the country-specific non-household rate, not an EU average.

**EV charging infrastructure at road freight depots:**

*Analytical inference:* Non-household electricity prices at €0.2264/kWh (Germany) versus €0.0748/kWh (Finland) represent a ~3x difference in per-kWh charging cost for electric handling equipment and road fleet charging. For workspaces with road-secondary operations across multiple EU markets, depot-level electricity cost is a material input into total cost of electrification. This is particularly relevant as EU truck CO₂ standards (under active rulemaking) are expected to push road fleet electrification timelines forward.

**Grid-connected vs. on-site generation — general EU feasibility:**

*Analytical inference:* On-site renewable generation and power purchase agreements (PPAs) are legally available across EU member states as tools to reduce exposure to grid pricing. The specific permitting, grid connection, and PPA regulatory conditions vary by member state and are not addressed by the Eurostat source. No cross-border restriction on on-site solar was identified in available sources. Regulatory feasibility details for specific countries require in-country legal and planning review.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether on-site generation qualifies for industrial electricity tax relief or levy exemptions in specific EU member states — particularly Germany, where non-network cost components (levies, renewable surcharges) are a significant driver of the high headline rate — requires country-level legal review. The Eurostat data reflects prices net of refundable taxes and levies for non-household consumers, but the specific recovery mechanisms differ by jurisdiction.

---

**Coverage note:** This brief covers industrial electricity prices across the EU as a cross-regional input for logistics and freight operations. The "region" is the EU as a collective industrial electricity market, with country-level variation highlighted where source data permits.

**EU non-household electricity prices — second half 2025 (FACT):**

Non-household electricity prices in the EU (defined as medium-sized consumers with annual consumption between 500 MWh and 2,000 MWh) were highest in Ireland (€0.2552 per kWh), Cyprus (€0.2429 per kWh), and Germany (€0.2264 per kWh) in the second half of 2025. The lowest prices were observed in Finland (€0.0748 per kWh) and Sweden (€0.0970 per kWh). The EU average price in the second half of 2025 was €0.1837 per kWh. *Source: Eurostat, Electricity Price Statistics (nrg_pc_205), data extracted April 2026. https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Electricity_price_statistics

**EU non-household price trajectory — 2025 year-on-year movement (FACT):**

Non-household electricity prices in the EU fell by 5.4% in the second half of 2025 compared to the same period in 2024, and by 3.5% from the first half of 2025. *Source: Eurostat, Electricity Price Statistics, data extracted April 2026. https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Electricity_price_statistics

**EU household price baseline — second half 2025 (FACT, included for context on tax structure affecting all consumers):**

The EU average household electricity price in the second half of 2025 was €0.2896 per kWh (including taxes), with taxes and levies representing 28.9% of that total. The highest household prices were in Ireland (€0.4042 per kWh) and Germany (€0.3869 per kWh); the lowest were in Hungary (€0.1082 per kWh) and Malta (€0.1282 per kWh). *Source: Eurostat, Electricity Price Statistics (nrg_pc_204), data extracted April 2026. https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Electricity_price_statistics

**Country-level spread within the EU — operational significance:**

*Analytical inference:* The 3.4x spread between Finland (€0.0748/kWh) and Ireland (€0.2552/kWh) for non-household consumers in H2 2025 is operationally material for any freight-forwarding workspace evaluating where to locate energy-intensive ground operations, consolidation hubs, or temperature-controlled warehousing within the EU. Workspaces with flexibility on EU hub location — for example, those routing through multiple European gateways for air cargo, live events, or high-value automotive cargo — face electricity cost differentials large enough to affect unit economics at scale.

*Operational implication:* Germany, which carries some of the highest non-household electricity costs in the EU (€0.2264/kWh), is simultaneously a dominant air and road freight hub. Workspaces operating energy-intensive facilities (cold chain, charging infrastructure for electric handling equipment, or on-site data systems for track-and-trace) at German gateway airports or logistics parks face structurally higher electricity cost exposure than equivalent operations in Finland or Sweden.

**IEA cross-regional comparison — labeled inference from described but inaccessible source blocks:**

*Analytical inference:* The IEA Electricity 2025 Executive Summary and Electricity Mid-Year Update 2025 are described as stating that EU industrial electricity prices in 2025 were approximately double US levels and approximately 50% above China levels, and that in 2019 the EU premium over the US was only approximately 50% before roughly doubling by 2025. These figures are sourced from IEA publications listed as corroborators below. Because the IEA source pages were blocked by Cloudflare at retrieval time and no verbatim span is available from those blocks, these specific ratios cannot be FACT-grounded in this brief. They are flagged here as high-priority candidates for source retrieval; when IEA pages become accessible, the 2x US / 1.5x China differential should be span-grounded and promoted to FACT status in the next regeneration.

*Specific IEA cross-regional price ratios (2019–2025) not available from primary sources as of 2026-05-27 — Cloudflare block prevented content extraction from all IEA source blocks.*

---

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

1. EU non-household electricity prices fell 5.4% year-on-year in H2 2025, suggesting peak crisis-era energy surcharges may ease — but prices remain above pre-2021 levels and vary 3.4x across EU member states. (*FACT-grounded; citable to Eurostat April 2026 data.*)

2. For clients with EU manufacturing or distribution operations, the country-level spread in electricity costs (Finland €0.0748/kWh vs. Ireland €0.2552/kWh in H2 2025) is now large enough to be a named factor in network design conversations, particularly as cold chain, electric vehicle charging, and digital infrastructure raise facility electricity consumption.

3. EU industrial electricity costs are structurally higher than the US equivalent — a relevant input when clients ask why EU-side consolidation or value-added services carry higher unit costs than US-side alternatives.

**What to avoid claiming in client conversations:**

- Do not cite the specific IEA cross-regional ratios (2x US, 1.5x China) as confirmed fact in client-facing materials until the IEA source pages are accessible and span-grounded. Carry them as directional context only.
- Do not present the H2 2025 price decline as a trend reversal. Eurostat data shows EU non-household prices remain above pre-crisis levels; a single-semester decline does not establish a sustained downward trend.
- Do not quote per-kWh prices for specific countries as current operational inputs without dating them precisely (H2 2025, Eurostat nrg_pc_205). Energy prices update semi-annually; a price cited without a date becomes a liability.

**Question to pose to clients with EU distribution footprints:**

"Has your EU facility network been evaluated against the country-level electricity cost spread since 2022? The gap between the highest and lowest-cost EU markets for industrial electricity is now approximately 3.4x — that's a material input into the economics of consolidation, cold chain, and any electrification programme."

---

In the second half of 2025, compared with the second half of 2024, household electricity prices in the EU showed the highest increase in Romania (58.6%). The largest decrease was observed in Cyprus (-14.7%). Electricity prices for non-household consumers in the EU fell by 5.4% in the second half of 2025 compared to the same period in 2024 and by 3.5% from the first half of 2025. Non-household electricity prices in the EU were highest in Ireland (€0.2552 per kWh) and lowest in Finland (€0.0748 per kWh) in the second half of 2025. Source: Eurostat ( nrg_pc_204 ) This article highlights the development of electricity prices both for household and non-household consumers within the European Union (EU) . When available, it also includes price data from Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania, Serbia, Türkiye, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo*, Moldova, Georgia and Ukraine. The price of energy in the EU depends on a range of different supply and demand conditions, including the geopolitical situation, the national energy mix, import diversification, network costs, environmental protection costs, severe weather conditions, or levels of excise and taxation. Note that the prices presented in this article include taxes, levies and VAT for household consumers, but exclude refundable taxes and levies for non-household consumers. * This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo declaration of independence. Electricity prices for household consumers Highest electricity prices in Ireland and Germany For household consumers in the EU (defined for the purpose of this article as medium-sized consumers with an annual consumption between 2 500  Kilowatt-hours (kWh) and 5 000 kWh), electricity prices in the second half of 2025 were highest in Ireland (€0.4042 per kWh), Germany (€0.3869 per kWh), Belgium (€0.3499 per kWh), and Denmark (€0.3312 per kWh) - see Figure 1. The lowest prices were observed in Hungary (€0.1082 per kWh), Malta (€0.1282 per kWh) and Bulgaria (€0.1355 per kWh). For Irish household consumers, the per kWh cost was 40% above the EU average price, whereas households in Hungary, Malta and Bulgaria paid less than half the price of the EU average. The EU average price in the second half of 2025 – a weighted average using the most recent (2024) consumption data for electricity by household consumers – was €0.2896 per kWh. Figure 1: Electricity prices for household consumers, second half 2025 Source: Eurostat ( nrg_pc_204 ) Figure 2 depicts the development of electricity prices for household consumers in the EU since the first half of 2008. The price without taxes, i.e. the energy, supply and network, was relatively stable between 2016 and 2020. The prices rose sharply in both semesters of 2022 and reached a peak of €0.2385 per kWh in the first half of 2023. In the second half of 2023, the price excluding taxes fell to €0.2244 per kWh. After that, prices broadly stabilised - remaining above pre crisis levels - at €0.2222 per kWh in the first half of 2024 and €0.2175 per kWh in the second half of 2024. The downward trend continued in 2025, reaching €0.2075 per kWh in the first half and €0.2059 per kWh in the second half. Electricity prices including taxes for household consumers rose steadily after 2021, with the only interruption being a fall in the second half of 2023. Prices then peaked in the first half of 2024 at €0.2916 per kWh, before edging down to €0.2887 in the second half of 2024 and €0.2879 in the first half of 2025. In the second half of 2025, prices ticked up slightly to €0.2896 per kWh, still 0.7% below the first-half 2024 peak. The percentage of taxes in the total price increased by almost 10 percentage points (pp) from 31.2% in the first half of 2008 to 41.0% in the second half of 2019. After this point, it substantially decreased until the second half of 2022 (14.7%), when taxes were the lowest in the entire period for which data are available. Moderate and stable tax increases have been recorded in 2023, 2024 and 2025, reaching 28.9% in the second half of the year. These figures reflect the impact of the governmental measures to mitigate EU household electricity costs in 2022 and the gradual reduction of those measures since 2023. This reduction of consumer relief measures, reflected in Figure 2 as gradual increase of taxes, explains the widening gap, between the two time-series of prices- those with taxes and those without-since 2023. Figure 2: Development of electricity prices for household consumers, EU, 2008-2025 Source: Eurostat ( nrg_pc_204 ) Weight of taxes and levies differs greatly between EU countries Figure 3 shows the proportion of taxes and levies in the overall electricity retail price for household consumers. In the EU, the share of taxes in the second half of 2025 was the lowest in Luxembourg and the Netherlands, where the values were in fact negative (-6.3% and -5.2%, respectively). The relative share of taxes was highest in Denmark, making up 49.1% of the total price. The average share of total taxes and levies at EU level in the second half of 2025 was 28.9%, an increase of 1.3 pp when compared with the first half of 2025, mostly driven by reduction of subsidies and allowances. The VAT in the EU represented 15.2% of the total price. It ranged from 4.8% in Malta to 21.3% in Hungary. Figure 3: Share of taxes and levies paid by household consumers for electricity, second half 2025 Source: Eurostat ( nrg_pc_204 ) Largest increase in electricity prices in Romania and Austria Figure 4 shows the percentage change in electricity prices for household consumers including all taxes and VAT between the second half of 2025 and the second half of 2024. For comparison purposes, the national currencies were used. For energy prices, comparing year on year instead of semester on semester is most meaningful to avoid seasonal effects. However, these seasonal effects are less prominent in the recent semesters. Year on year, the total prices increased in 17 of the EU countries, while they decreased in 10 EU countries. The largest increase was observed in Romania (58.6%), followed by Austria (34.3%) and Ireland (32.7%). Mainly network costs, as well as the reduction of subsidies and allowances drove the increase. Cyprus (-14.7%), France (-12.5%) and Denmark (-11.9%) were the 3 EU countries to record the largest decreases. Figure 4: Change in electricity prices for household consumers compared with previous year same semester, (National currency) second half 2025 Source: Eurostat ( nrg_pc_204 ) Electricity prices in purchasing power standard In Map 1, electricity prices for household consumers in the second half of 2025 are shown in purchasing power standard (PPS) , grouping the available countries in 6 categories, with electricity price categories ranging from 14.09 PPS per 100 kWh to 49.52 PPS per 100 kWh. Electricity prices based on PPS were highest in Romania (49.52), Czechia (38.65) and Poland (37.15). The lowest electricity prices based on the purchasing power standard were observed in Malta (14.09), Hungary (15.10) and Finland (18.77). Map 1: Electricity prices for household consumers, second semester of 2025 Source: Eurostat ( nrg_pc_204 ) Share of transmission and distribution costs for household electricity consumers Figure 5 presents the share of transmission and distribution costs for household electricity consumers. Transmission and distribution costs are only reported once a year, at the end of the second semester. Distribution costs account for the largest share by far, when compared with the transmission costs. This is normal for all types of networks including the electricity system. Transmission network is used for transmitting bulk amounts of energy over long distances. The distribution network is usually the part of the system where the consumers are connected. The distribution network is denser than the transmission network, therefore, its share in the costs is expected to be higher. Countries with lower population density require a more extensive transmission network to meet their needs. Their costs are higher when compared with the countries with higher population density. Smaller, densely populated countries use mostly their own distribution network. The latest available data for transmission and distribution costs are for the year 2025, in which, Luxembourg (100.0%), Slovakia (91.5%) and Finland (90.0%) had the highest shares of distribution costs. On the other hand, Lithuania (43.5%), Estonia (33.0%) and Denmark (32.0%) had the highest shares of transmission costs. Figure 5: Share of transmission and distribution costs paid by household consumers for electricity, 2025 Source: Eurostat ( nrg_pc_206 ) Electricity prices for non-household consumers Electricity prices highest in Ireland and Cyprus Non-household consumers are defined for the purpose of this article as medium-sized consumers with an annual consumption between 500 MWh (Mega Watt hours) and 2 000 MWh. As depicted in Figure 6, electricity prices in the second half of 2025 were highest in Ireland (€0.2552 per kWh), Cyprus (€0.2429 per kWh) and Germany(€0.2264 per kWh). The lowest prices were observed in Finland (€0.0748 per kWh) and Sweden (€0.0970 per kWh). The EU average price in the second half of 2025 was €0.1837 per kWh. The aggregates are weighted averages taking into consideration the average consumption in each band. Figure 6: Electricity prices for non-household consumers, second half 2025 Source: Eurostat ( nrg_pc_205 ) Figure 7 shows the development of electricity prices for non-household consumers in the EU since the first half of 2008. The price without taxes, i.e. the energy, supply and network, underwent minor fluctuations until 2021. After this point in time, during the second half of 2021 and even more so, throughout both halves of 2022, the price registered significant increases, peaking at €0.1987 per kWh in the second half of 2022. Subsequently, in both halves of 2023 (€0.1938 per kWh in the first half and €0.1767 per kWh in the second) as well as the first half of 2024 (€0.1575 per kWh), the price recorded declines. In the second half of 2024, prices excluding taxes showed a marginal increase for the first time since the peak, reaching €0.1629 per kWh. However, in the first half of 2025 prices excluding taxes decreased to €0.1570 per kWh, and further decreased in the second half to €0.1511, which is the lowest since the beginning of 2022. The proportion of taxes rose by 21.0 pp, from 13.8% in the first half of 2008 to 34.8% in the first half of 2020, before declining. By the first half of 2024, the share of taxes had fallen to 16.4%, and further decreased to 16.1% in the second half, reflecting an increase from the lowest point of 5.7% recorded in the second half of 2022. In the first half of 2025, the proportion of taxes increased to 17.5%, and to 17.7% in the second half. Looking at the non-household total price, i.e. including non-recoverable taxes, the increase persisted for an additional semester compared with the price excluding taxes and peaked at €0.2151 per kWh in the first half of 2023. In the second half of 2023, the price declined (€0.2003 per kWh), followed by a further drop in the first half of 2024 (€0.1885 per kWh). In the second half of 2024, the price rose by 2.9% to €0.1941 per kWh. It then eased again, falling to €0.1903 per kWh in the first half of 2025 and to €0.1837 per kWh in the second half of 2025, a further 3.5% decline. *Analytical inference:* ### METI Subcommittee on ETS — Final Report Issued December 2025

*Analytical inference:* The METI Subcommittee on Emissions Trading Systems released its final report on 19 December 2025, covering benchmarks, grandfathering, price limits, and compliance structure for Phase 2. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

*Operational implication:* The subcommittee's work on system coverage and compliance structure included consideration of whether closely related entities — such as parent companies and subsidiaries — should be treated as a single compliance unit under the system. This remains a design variable with operational significance for vertically integrated transport and logistics groups operating in Japan. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

### Banking Rules — Under Examination

*Analytical inference:* Banking of allowances: there are currently no regulations for banking in place, but the government is examining the possibility of implementing banking rules in FY2027. Borrowing is not allowed. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Analytical inference:* Resolution of banking rules in FY2027 will affect allowance management strategies for covered transport-sector entities. Workspace carrier partners should be asked about their allowance position and banking exposure once rules are finalised.

### Phase 3 Auctioning — From FY2033

*Analytical inference:* From FY2033, auctioning will be introduced for high-emitting corporations in the power sector. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets In Phase 3, expected to begin from FY2033, a phased introduction of paid auctions for the power generation sector is planned. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

*Analytical inference:* Phase 3 auctioning is currently scoped to the power sector. Re-check window: monitor for any extension of auctioning to transport sectors during Phase 2 (FY2026–FY2032) policy reviews.

### GX-Surcharge on Fossil Fuels — From FY2028

A GX-Surcharge on fuel imports and domestic fossil fuel extractors is planned from FY2028. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Operational implication:* The GX-Surcharge, when introduced in FY2028, will affect fossil fuel costs for transport operators in Japan. This is distinct from ETS allowance costs and will represent an additional carbon pricing layer. COST ALERT: re-check window FY2028 for surcharge rate publication.

---

### 1. Emissions Data Infrastructure

**Scope:** If the workspace or its carrier partners are Phase 2 covered entities, a facility-level CO₂ measurement and reporting system is required, aligned to the GX Promotion Act MRV framework.

**Deadline:** Annual submission by 31 January. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Operational implication:* Workspaces not directly covered should nonetheless build capacity to request and receive verified CO₂ data from Japan-based carrier partners, as this data will underpin Scope 3 emissions reporting to clients operating under CSRD, ISSB, or equivalent disclosure frameworks.

**Gap from current baseline:** *Analytical inference:* Freight forwarding operations typically rely on spend-based or distance-based emissions estimation for Scope 3. Japan GX-ETS carrier MRV data, once available from covered carriers, would represent a more granular activity-based data source. The gap between current estimation practice and carrier-verified activity data should be assessed.

### 2. Third-Party Verification Alignment

**Scope:** Phase 2 emissions reports require third-party verification by an accredited verifier. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Operational implication:* Workspace carrier partners in Japan transport sectors will need to engage accredited verifiers. This creates a procurement and lead-time consideration for carriers; workspace procurement teams should factor verifier availability into carrier readiness assessments.

### 3. Allowance Management (if covered)

*Legal Confirmation Required:* If the workspace is determined to be a covered entity, it will need an allowance management system — tracking allocations (benchmark or grandfathering basis), monitoring trading positions against upper (JPY 4,300 FY2026/FY2027) and lower (JPY 1,700 FY2026/FY2027) price limits, and managing the annual compliance surrender cycle. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets This requirement attaches only if covered entity status is confirmed by counsel.

### 4. Offset Credit Management (if covered)

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Covered entities may use domestic J-Credits and international JCM credits as offsets, subject to a cap of 10% of the entity's compliance obligation. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets Workspace operations should track this cap if covered entity status is confirmed.

---

This brief covers Japan's Green Transformation (GX) League framework as it applies to freight transport operations, with particular focus on transport-sector participation requirements, emissions trading obligations, and the transition from voluntary to mandatory phases. The document synthesises across five corpus sources as of the date of generation.

**Convention notes:**
- "GX League" refers to the voluntary framework launched in FY2023 under the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI).
- "GX-ETS" refers to the emissions trading system nested within and evolving from the GX League.
- "FY" refers to Japan's fiscal year, running April–March (e.g., FY2023 = April 2023–March 2024).
- "Phase 1" = FY2023–FY2025 (voluntary); "Phase 2" = FY2026–FY2032 (mandatory); "Phase 3" = from FY2033.
- All monetary figures are in Japanese Yen (JPY) unless otherwise noted.
- *Legal Confirmation Required:* callouts flag conclusions that turn on legal interpretation, not this document.

---

### Supply Chain Position

The GX League and GX-ETS are company-level frameworks. Covered entities are companies — specifically those meeting emissions thresholds — not cargo principals or freight forwarders acting as intermediaries per se.

*Operational implication:* In Japan transport operations, the compliance-obligated entity under Phase 2 is most likely the carrier — the operator of freight automobile transport, domestic marine transport, or air transport — not the freight forwarder or shipper, unless the forwarder directly operates covered transport assets. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether any role the workspace occupies — as freight forwarder, importer, or logistics coordinator — constitutes a "covered entity" under the GX Promotion Act, or whether compliance obligations pass-through contractually from carrier to customer, requires counsel review. The sourced materials define coverage by direct CO₂ emissions volume, not by commercial intermediary role.

### Indirect Exposure Pathways

*Operational implication:* Even if the workspace is not a directly obligated entity, three indirect exposure pathways are present:
1. **Cost pass-through**: Carrier compliance costs under the GX-ETS (allowance purchases, MRV costs) are likely to be incorporated into freight pricing on Japan lanes over FY2026–FY2032. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets
2. **Scope 3 reporting**: Workspace clients operating under CSRD, ISSB, or equivalent disclosure frameworks may request Japan transport emissions data at carrier-activity level for Scope 3 accounting.
3. **Supply chain GX League expectations**: The GX League framework explicitly encompasses discussions on emissions reductions throughout the supply chain and the input of green products into the market. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

### Position of NYK as a Reference Operator

NYK Line announced its participation in the GX League in June 2023, citing alignment with METI's GX League Basic Concept and stating it had set a long-term goal of reducing GHG emissions in its oceangoing shipping business to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. *Source: NYK to Join Japanese Ministry's GX League, NYK Line, 9 June 2023. https://www.nyk.com/english/news/2023/20230607_01.html

*Operational implication:* Ocean carrier partners operating on Japan trade lanes who are GX League participants will be subject to self-set emission reduction targets and, from Phase 2, mandatory compliance obligations. Workspace Japan lane ocean freight procurement should factor in carrier compliance posture.

---

### Question 1: Is the workspace a "covered entity" under Phase 2?

**Status:** *Legal Confirmation Required:* Phase 2 coverage turns on whether a company's annual CO₂ emissions meet or exceed 100,000 tonnes. The obligation is statutory under the amended GX Promotion Act. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560 Whether freight forwarding or logistics coordination activity generates direct emissions meeting this threshold, or whether the threshold applies only to the asset operator, requires counsel and emissions-accounting review.

### Question 2: Does the workspace's transport mode trigger transport-sector benchmarking?

**Status:** Benchmarking under Phase 2 applies to freight automobile transportation, domestic marine transportation, and air transportation. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets *Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether the workspace or its carrier partners fall into one of these named benchmark categories, or into the residual grandfathering category, requires assessment against actual transport operations and legal review.

### Question 3: Does the GX League voluntary participation create commercial or contractual expectations?

**Decided — with sourced basis:** The GX League explicitly encompasses supply chain emissions reduction discussions. Active discussions on and proposals for rulemaking have been held regarding areas such as emissions reductions throughout the supply chain and the input of green products into the market. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html *Operational implication:* Carrier partners who are GX League participants may increasingly request or expect supply chain GHG data from freight principals, including freight forwarders acting on behalf of shippers.

### Question 4: Does voluntary Phase 1 non-registration carry consequences?

**Decided — with sourced basis:** METI stated it would consider companies that have no intention to register their data and those that do not respond to the communications from the Secretariat as having withdrawn from the league as of the end of June 2024. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html This is a reputational/participation consequence, not a statutory penalty in the Phase 1 voluntary period.

---

### Voluntary vs Mandatory — Phase 1 Carve-out

Phase 1 (FY2023–FY2025) is entirely voluntary. The mandatory Phase 2 obligation began in FY2026. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets Participation during Phase 1 does not automatically create Phase 2 obligations; Phase 2 coverage is determined by the 100,000-tonne threshold under the amended GX Promotion Act. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

### SME and Startup Support

The GX League provides meticulous support to participating companies, which vary in size and by industry, consisting of not only large enterprises but also SMEs and startups. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

*Operational implication:* SME and startup freight operators voluntarily participating in the GX League have access to a special consultation counter and tailored support, including explanations on how to calculate emissions. This reduces the barrier to voluntary participation for smaller transport operators.

### Upper Price Limit as Compliance Escape Valve

*Analytical inference:* When allowance prices rise above the established upper price limit, entities can meet their obligations by paying the upper limit. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets This is a price ceiling that caps the maximum compliance cost per tonne for covered entities.

*Analytical inference:* For transport-sector covered entities whose compliance cost exposure is uncertain, the upper price limit (JPY 4,300 for FY2026/FY2027, rising by approximately 3% CPI-linked annually from FY2027) provides a calculable worst-case cost ceiling per tonne of exceedance.

### International Linking — Excluded

*Analytical inference:* The GX-ETS will not be linked with any other system. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets International credits (JCM) are eligible as offsets within the 10% cap, but this is not ETS-linking. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

---

### What the GX League and GX-ETS Are

The GX League is a framework established by METI in which a group of internationally competitive companies that are boldly taking on the challenge of transitioning to carbon neutrality will drive GX (Green Transformation). *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

METI released the "GX League Basic Concept" on 1 February 2022, and the GX League was launched in FY2023. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

The GX League works as a framework covering over 50% of the greenhouse gas emissions in Japan. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

*Analytical inference:* Japan started its GX-ETS as a voluntary baseline-and-credit system during its first phase spanning FY2023 and FY2025. In FY2026, which started in April 2026, the GX-ETS transitioned to a mandatory baseline-and-credit system. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, International Carbon Action Partnership (ICAP). https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

**effective_date covered:** The GX League was launched in FY2023 (April 2023). *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

**jurisdictional_scope covered:** The framework applies in Japan, across multiple sectors including maritime domestic aviation, transport, industry, and power. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

### Transport Sector's Specific Position Within the GX League

From FY2024, companies from the transport industry — including air transport, railway transport, and land transport — newly joined the league. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

Sectoral coverage under the GX-ETS includes Maritime, Domestic Aviation, Transport, Industry, and Power. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

For Phase 2 (FY2026 onwards), benchmarking applies specifically to: freight automobile transportation, domestic marine transportation, and air transportation — among other sectors. Other transport-adjacent sectors receive allocation based on grandparenting. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

### Why This Applies to the Workspace

*Operational implication:* Freight forwarding operations with Japan trade lanes, and particularly those acting as or engaging with carriers operating in the air, road, or maritime transport sectors, are within the sectoral scope of the GX-ETS. The transport sector is among those named explicitly in both the voluntary GX League and the mandatory Phase 2 obligation. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether any specific entity — including a freight forwarder, logistics operator, or shipper — meets the defined compliance-obligated status under Phase 2 of the GX-ETS (i.e., whether it is a "covered entity" as defined by the GX Promotion Act) depends on its direct CO₂ emissions threshold and legal relationship to covered facilities. Counsel review is required to determine whether Phase 2 obligations attach to any given workspace role.

---

### Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM) — International Decarbonisation Pathway

*Analytical inference:* Japan's Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM) is a bilateral scheme to incentivize decarbonizing technologies and mitigation actions in 31 partner countries. JCM credits are eligible for use in the GX-ETS. Separately, 90 partner countries and over 300 organizations have joined Japan's global capacity-building initiative, the Article 6 Implementation Partnership. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Operational implication:* For freight operations on Japan trade lanes that also span JCM partner countries, there may be dual value in JCM-eligible decarbonisation investments — both reducing emissions and generating offset credits usable within the GX-ETS compliance framework.

### Tokyo and Saitama Sub-National ETSs

*Analytical inference:* Sub-national ETSs operate in Tokyo and Saitama. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Analytical inference:* Transport operations concentrated in the Tokyo or Saitama metropolitan areas may face overlapping sub-national ETS requirements in addition to the national GX-ETS. Workspaces with Japan gateway operations through Tokyo-area facilities should assess sub-national exposure separately.

### Industry Coalition Positioning

Japan Climate Initiative (JCI) and Japan Climate Leaders Partnership (JCLP) are assessed as supporting GX-ETS Phase 2, with active and strategic engagement respectively. Japan Business Federation (Keidanren) is characterised as mixed. Japan Iron and Steel Federation (JISF), Japan Chemical Industry Association (JCIA), and Electric Power Development (J-Power) are characterised as not supporting. Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA) and Toyota Motor are characterised as mixed. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

*Analytical inference:* Transport-sector industry associations (road, automotive) present mixed-to-not-supporting positions on the mandatory ETS. This indicates the design of benchmarks and grandfathering for the transport sector may evolve through continued lobbying during Phase 2. Workspace commercial teams should monitor for sector-specific rule adjustments.

---

### Phase 1 (FY2023–FY2025) — Voluntary

*Analytical inference:* **Participation basis:** Companies participating in the GX League set their own emission targets and were required to calculate and report their actual emissions. Companies that failed to meet their self-set targets were required to purchase specified carbon credits or explain the reasons for their failure. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

**GX League participant obligations (Phase 1):** Participants upheld their own targets of emission reductions not only for FY2030 but also for FY2025, and decided to participate in an emissions trading system currently being operated on a trial basis. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

**Offset use in Phase 1:** The use of offset credits was allowed. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

### Phase 2 (FY2026–FY2032) — Mandatory

*Analytical inference:* **Inclusion threshold:** Companies with annual CO₂ emissions of 100,000 tonnes or more in power, industry, transport and aviation as well as in other sectors if their annual CO₂ emissions exceed the 100,000 tonnes threshold. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

**Point of regulation:** Point source; type of entities: Companies. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Analytical inference:* **Cap structure:** A bottom-up absolute cap limits the total emissions allowed in the system and is fixed ex-ante. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

**Allocation — transport benchmarking sectors:** Benchmarking applies for freight automobile transportation, domestic marine transportation, and air transportation. Allocation based on grandparenting applies to other sectors. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

**Compliance obligation:** Covered entities surrender one compliance unit per tCO₂ that exceeds the facility's annual emissions limit. Compliance period: one year. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

**Penalty:** If the required number of allowances cannot be surrendered, a payment equal to the shortfall in emission allowances × upper price × 1.1 must be made. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Analytical inference:* **Price controls:**
- Upper price limit in FY2027: JPY 4,300 (USD 28.73). When allowance prices rise above the established upper price limit, entities can meet their obligations by paying the upper limit. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets
- Lower price limit in FY2027: JPY 1,700 (USD 11.36). When a certain number of days pass with trading prices below the lower limit, a reverse auction will be held to balance the supply and demand for allowances. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets
- For FY2026, the Reference Upper Limit Transaction Price is 4,300 yen per carbon-dioxide-emission-quota unit; the Adjustment Standard Transaction Price is 1,700 yen per carbon-dioxide-emission-quota unit. From FY2027 to FY2030, prices are adjusted annually by applying a 3% increase to the projected consumer price index. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

**Offset use in Phase 2:** The use of offset credits is allowed. Domestic (J-Credits) and international (JCM credits) credits are allowed with quantitative limits. The use of offset credits is capped at 10% of an entity's compliance obligation. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Analytical inference:* **Banking and borrowing:** There are currently no regulations for banking in place, but the government is examining the possibility of implementing banking rules in FY2027. Borrowing is not allowed. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Analytical inference:* **Linking:** The GX-ETS will not be linked with any other system. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Analytical inference:* **GHGs covered:** CO₂. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

### GHG Reduction Targets (National Context)

*Analytical inference:* By FY2030: 46% reduction from FY2013 GHG levels, including LULUCF credits; and continue efforts to cut emissions by 50%. By 2050: Net zero GHG emissions. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

### GX-Surcharge (from FY2028)

*Analytical inference:* A carbon levy (GX-Surcharge) to be introduced from 2028 on fossil fuel importers and domestic fossil fuel extractors. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Operational implication:* The GX-Surcharge is an additional carbon pricing layer that will affect fuel costs for transport operators using fossil fuels, distinct from the ETS allowance mechanism. COST ALERT: monitor FY2028 for surcharge rate and pass-through mechanism.

### Auctioning Trajectory (Power Sector)

*Analytical inference:* From FY2033, auctioning will be introduced for high-emitting corporations in the power sector. Revenues from auctioning for power generation companies, together with revenues from the fossil fuel surcharge, will be used to redeem GX Economic Transition Bonds. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Analytical inference:* Auctioning for FY2033 is currently defined only for the power sector. No sourced evidence places transport sector auctioning on the current policy trajectory within the Phase 2 window (FY2026–FY2032).

---

### GX League Basic Concept (METI, 1 February 2022)

*Analytical inference:* The GX League Basic Concept established the framework philosophy: a place where companies actively engaged in GX are invited to collaborate with government, academia, and financial institutions to take up the challenge of GX, and engage in discussions for the transformation of the entire economic and social system and the creation of new markets. *Source: NYK to Join Japanese Ministry's GX League, NYK Line, 9 June 2023 (referencing METI website). https://www.nyk.com/english/news/2023/20230607_01.html

*Operational implication:* The Basic Concept is a framework document, not an enforcement instrument. Its significance is that it established the GX League's purpose and design principles, which subsequently underpinned the GX Promotion Act and the mandatory Phase 2 obligations.

### GX Promotion Act

*Analytical inference:* In May 2025, the amended GX Promotion Act (officially named: Bill for the Act for Partially Amending the Act on the Promoting Transition to the Decarbonized Growth Economic Structure and Act on the Promotion of Effective Utilization of Resources) was passed and enacted at the House of Councillors plenary session, obliging companies that emit at least 100,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide a year to participate in the emissions trading system to be introduced in fiscal year 2026. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

*Operational implication:* The amended GX Promotion Act is the binding statutory instrument for Phase 2. The GX League voluntary framework is a predecessor and parallel structure; the Act is the enforcement vehicle. Workspaces should distinguish between GX League membership (voluntary, reputational, supply-chain-facing) and GX-ETS compliance (statutory, from FY2026).

### MRV Framework Provisions

Under the GX Promotion Act, covered entities submit their emissions reports annually by 31 January of the year following the reporting year. Emissions reports require third-party verification by an accredited verifier. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

### Compliance Mechanism

Covered entities surrender one compliance unit per tCO₂ that exceeds the facility's annual emissions limit. If the required number of allowances cannot be surrendered, a payment equal to the shortfall in emission allowances × upper price × 1.1 must be made. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

**penalty_summary covered:** The enforcement penalty for Phase 2 covered entities is: payment equal to the shortfall in emission allowances × upper price × 1.1. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Operational implication:* For Phase 1 (FY2023–FY2025, voluntary), the GX League characterised non-compliance differently: companies from FY2023 that failed to meet self-set targets were required to purchase specified carbon credits or explain the reasons for their failure. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

For Phase 1 GX League voluntary participants that failed to register data and did not respond to Secretariat communications, METI stated it would consider them as having withdrawn from the league as of the end of June 2024. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

---

### GX League Voluntary Registration (Phase 1)

GX League participants are asked to register related data such as their emissions reduction targets. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

METI opened a special consultation counter on its official website to support companies in registering their data, providing tailored consultations including explanations on how to calculate emissions. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html

**primary_deadline covered (Phase 1 voluntary context):** No compliance deadline in the statutory sense: the GX League Phase 1 (FY2023–FY2025) is characterised as a voluntary framework with no mandated compliance date. However, METI set 30 June 2024 as the date after which non-responding participants would be treated as withdrawn. *Source: From FY2024, 179 Companies Newly Participate in the GX League, METI, 27 March 2024. https://www.meti.go.jp/english/press/2024/0327_003.html For Phase 2 (mandatory), the headline compliance deadline is the annual emissions report submission by 31 January of the year following the reporting year. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

### Phase 2 MRV Obligations (from FY2026)

Covered entities submit their emissions reports annually by 31 January of the year following the reporting year. Emissions reports require third-party verification by an accredited verifier. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

The regulatory framework for MRV is the GX Promotion Act. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

*Operational implication:* For workspace carrier partners who are Phase 2 covered entities, the annual reporting cycle (activity year → 31 January submission → third-party verification) creates a structured data availability window. Workspace Scope 3 reporting for Japan lanes could align to this cadence, but carrier-level data may not be available to freight forwarders until Q1 of the calendar year following the activity year.

### Institutional Administration

The GX Acceleration Agency has been established to carry out operations related to the ETS and the GX-Surcharge system. METI administers the implementation of the J-Credit and JCM schemes and is responsible for the GX League. The Ministry of the Environment administers the J-Credit and JCM schemes and is tasked with developing carbon pricing in Japan jointly with METI. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

### 1. Assess Phase 2 Inclusion Threshold — MONITORING

**Action:** Assess whether operations in Japan's transport sector generate direct CO₂ emissions at or above 100,000 tonnes per year, which is the Phase 2 inclusion threshold.

*Operational implication:* Phase 2 of the GX-ETS, which began in April 2026, covers companies with annual CO₂ emissions of 100,000 tonnes or more in power, industry, transport, and aviation. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets The mandatory phase is expected to apply to 300 to 400 companies. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether a freight forwarder or logistics operator acting on behalf of carrier clients meets the "covered entity" threshold, or whether obligations pass through to the freight principal, requires counsel review and cannot be determined from the sourced materials alone.

### 2. Verify Carrier and Supplier GX-ETS Compliance Status — MONITORING

**Action:** Verify whether ocean, air, and road carrier partners in Japan are participating in the GX League (voluntary phase) and, for Phase 2, whether they hold compliance obligations under the mandatory GX-ETS.

*Operational implication:* Carriers in transport sectors are specifically named as subject to benchmarking under Phase 2 allocation rules. Freight automobile transportation, domestic marine transportation, and air transportation each have benchmarking methodologies. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets Carrier compliance posture directly affects the workspace's ability to report Scope 3 emissions for Japan-routed freight.

### 3. Map Emissions Reporting Obligations Under MRV Framework — MONITORING

**Action:** Map current emissions data collection practices against the GX-ETS MRV framework requiring covered entities to submit emissions reports annually by 31 January of the year following the reporting year, with third-party verification by an accredited verifier.

*Operational implication:* If the workspace or its carrier partners are covered entities, this MRV timeline governs the reporting cycle. *Source: Japan GX-ETS, ICAP. https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/japan-gx-ets

### 4. Track METI Subcommittee Output — MONITORING

**Action:** Track the METI Subcommittee on Emissions Trading Systems, which concluded its first cycle in December 2025 and is determining key Phase 2 design elements including benchmarks, grandfathering, and price limits.

*Analytical inference:* On 19 December 2025, the subcommittee released its final report and set the Reference Upper Limit Transaction Price at 4,300 yen per carbon-dioxide-emission-quota unit for FY2026, and the Adjustment Standard Transaction Price at 1,700 yen per carbon-dioxide-emission-quota unit for FY2026. From FY2027 to FY2030, both prices are to be adjusted annually by applying a 3% increase to the projected consumer price index for the relevant fiscal year, using the price of the previous fiscal year as the baseline. *Source: GX-ETS Phase 2, InfluenceMap, December 2025. https://japan.influencemap.org/policy/GX-ETS-Phase-2-5560

METI hereby announces that 179 companies will newly participate in the league from FY2024. The GX League will continue to drive Japan’s GX (green transformation) by working as a framework covering over 50% of the greenhouse gas emissions in Japan. 1. Outline of the GX League The GX League is a framework in which a group of internationally competitive companies that are boldly taking on the challenge of transitioning to carbon neutrality will drive GX. As of FY2023, 568 companies have participated in the league. These companies have been making significant efforts to reduce emissions, upholding their own targets of emission reductions not only for FY2030 but also for FY2025, and have also decided to participate in an emissions trading system currently being operated on a trial basis. Moreover, active discussions on and proposals for rulemaking, which is difficult for individual companies to undertake, have been held regarding areas such as emissions reductions throughout the supply chain and the input of green products into the market. 2. New participants from FY2024 In January 2024, the GX League opened a call for new companies that intend to participate in the league from FY2024 and received applications. As a result, 179 companies newly decided to participate in the league from FY2024, bringing the total number of participants to 747. From FY2024, these companies from a wide variety of industries, including the transport industry (including air transport, railway transport, and land transport), manufacturing industry (e.g., semiconductors), real estate industry, and information and communications industry, will join the league. The GX League will continue to drive Japan’s GX by working as a framework covering over 50% of the greenhouse gas emissions in Japan. Appendix 1: List of FY2024 new participants (in Japanese)(PDF:477KB) Appendix 2: Current state of the participants in the league (case examples by industry) (in Japanese)(PDF:350KB) 3. Supporting participants that have yet to submit their data The GX League asks participants to register related data such as their emissions reduction targets. However, some participants from FY2023 have not yet registered their data for a variety of reasons. To address this situation, the GX League has opened a special consultation counter on its official website as a measure to support such companies in registering their data, which provides services such as tailored consultations, including explanations on how to calculate emissions. The GX League will continue to provide meticulous support to participating companies, which vary in size and by industry, consisting of not only large enterprises but also SMEs and startups, so that these participants will be able to advance their efforts through the activities offered by the league. For details, visit the special webpage on the GX League official website. Note: The GX League will consider companies that have no intention to register their data and those that do not respond to the communications from the Secretariat as having withdrawn from the league as of the end of June 2024. In the FY2026, which started in April 2026, the GX-ETS transitioned to a mandatory baseline-and-credit system. Under the GX-ETS, allowances are traded on the market. Upper and lower price limits apply. From FY2033, auctioning will be introduced for high-emitting corporations in the power sector. More than 700 companies, accounting for over 50% of national GHG emissions, participated in the voluntary ETS. Japan combines several carbon pricing instruments to help achieve net zero emissions by 2050: an existing carbon tax, the ETS, and a carbon levy (GX-Surcharge) to be introduced from 2028 on fossil fuel importers and domestic fossil fuel extractors. Plans for this are outlined in the Basic Plan for the “Green Transformation (GX) Policy”, Japan’s ten-year decarbonization strategy. Japan is actively participating in international carbon markets. Its Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM) is a bilateral scheme to incentivize decarbonizing technologies and mitigation actions in 31 partner countries. JCM credits are eligible for use in the GX-ETS. Separately, 90 partner countries and over 300 organizations have joined Japan’s global capacity-building initiative, the Article 6 Implementation Partnership. Year in Review The mandatory GX-ETS began in April 2026, following a three-year voluntary phase and the adoption of the “Amended GX Promotion Act” by the Upper House of the Parliament in May 2025. Background The first phase of Japan’s Green Transformation emissions trading system (GX-ETS) took effect in fiscal 2023, whereby companies participated voluntarily within the GX League . Companies participating in the GX League set their own emission targets and were required to calculate and report their actual emissions. Companies that failed to meet their self-set targets were required to purchase specified carbon credits or explain the reasons for their failure. GX-ETS Phase 2 In May 2025, the amended GX Promotion Act (Officially named as: Bill for the Act for Partially Amending the Act on the Promoting Transition to the Decarbonized Growth Economic Structure and Act on the Promotion of Effective Utilization of Resources) was passed and enacted at the House of Councillors plenary session, obliging companies that emit at least 100,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide a year to participate in the emissions trading system to be introduced in fiscal (FY) 2026. According to the bill of GX Promotion Act, the new obligation is expected to apply to 300 to 400 companies with 100,000 tons of emissions, this includes steelmaking, auto, utility and chemicals. These rules will apply in Phase 2 of GX-ETS set to begin in FY2026 with more details still under consideration under the METI committee . In Phase 3, expected to begin from FY2033, a phased introduction of paid auctions for the power generation sector is planned. METI Subcommittee on the ETS Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) has established a Subcommittee on Emissions Trading Systems to deliberate on the technical design of the upcoming emissions trading system (ETS), following the revision of the GX Promotion Act. The first meeting was held in July 2025, and discussions are expected to conclude by the end of the year. Key issues under discussion include: System coverage and compliance strucure : Consideration of whether closely related entities — such as parent companies and subsidiaries — should be treated as a single compliance unit under the system. Monitoring Reporting, and Verification : Scope of covered greenhouse gases, calculation methodologies, treatment of carbon credits, accreditation requirements for third-party verification bodies, and assurance levels. Allowance allocation : Choice between benchmarking and grandfathering approaches; treatment of new entrants, facility closures, or changes in production activity; and possible adjustments for early reduction efforts, carbon leakage risks, and R&D investment. Price Control and Market Design : Conditions for triggering upper and lower price limits, and rules governing the deemed surrender of allowances — i.e., fulfilling compliance obligations through payment at the upper price threshold. On December 19, 2025, the subcommittee released its final report and requested that the Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry establish the Reference Upper Limit Transaction Price and the Adjustment Standard Transaction Price based on the following opinions: For fiscal year 2026, the Reference Upper Limit Transaction Price shall be set at 4,300 yen per carbon-dioxide-emission-quota unit for decarbonized growth-oriented investment, which is equivalent to one ton of CO2 emissions. For fiscal year 2026, the Adjustment Standard Transaction Price shall be set at 1,700 yen per carbon-dioxide-emission-quota unit for decarbonized growth-oriented investment, which is equivalent to one ton of CO2 emissions. For the period from fiscal year 2027 to fiscal year 2030, the Reference Upper Limit Transaction Price and the Adjustment Standard Transaction Price shall be updated and determined annually in accordance with the law; these prices shall be adjusted by applying a 3% increase to the projected consumer price index for the relevant fiscal year, using the price of the previous fiscal year as the baseline. Expected to be fully operational this fiscal year, the GX League is a place where companies that are working to realize sustainable growth through GX (Green Transformation) will work together with similar companies, government agencies, and universities to take on the challenges of GX (Green Transformation) and put them into practice to transform economic and social systems and create new markets. In September 2021, the NYK Group set a long-term goal of reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the Group’s oceangoing shipping business to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, and the company has since been implementing various fuel-saving and GHG reduction activities with the cooperation of various stakeholders, including customers. We are actively engaged in fuel-saving and GHG-reduction activities, the promotion of the use of LNG as marine fuel, and research and demonstration projects for the practical use of zero-emission fuels such as hydrogen and ammonia. On March 10, the NYK Group released its medium-term management plan “Sail Green, Drive Transformations 2026 — A Passion for Planetary Wellbeing.” The NYK Group is promoting growth strategies with ESG at the core, based on the Group’s basic philosophy of “Bringing value to life” and a new corporate vision for 2030, which reads, “we go beyond the scope of a comprehensive global logistics enterprise to co-create value required for the future by advancing our core business and growing new ones.” We believe that our efforts are in line with the objectives of the GX League following our endorsement of the "GX League Basic Concept" announced by METI in 2022. Through our participation in the GX League, we will further accelerate co-creation with various stakeholders and contribute to the realization of a carbon-neutral society and the transformation of economic and social systems. An outline of GX and the GX League is as follows (taken from METI website): GX (Green Transformation) Aims to transform the entire economic and social system by taking up the challenge of quickly transitioning to decarbonization, viewing the response to achieving decarbonization in Japan and the world as a growth opportunity. GX League A place where companies actively engaged in GX are invited to collaborate with government, academia, and financial institutions to take up the challenge of GX, and engage in discussions for the transformation of the entire economic and social system and the creation of new markets.
