sections.md:
**Sector-specific quantitative outputs are not in the supplied source blocks.** The source material covers the initiative's design, governance, and headline statistics. The ITF's in-depth sectoral studies covering road freight transport, maritime transport, and aviation — which would contain quantitative mitigation potentials, cost curves, and policy instrument comparisons for the modes the workspace operates — are not included in the supplied sources. Those outputs are catalogued in the initiative's Publications and Outputs section but were not provided. The workspace cannot derive mode-specific compliance cost estimates or mitigation pathway quantification from the present brief.

**The brief does not resolve what specific policy outputs have been adopted from ITF analysis.** The ITF initiative identifies options for decision-makers; it does not itself mandate policies. The chain from ITF analysis to a specific adopted regulation (e.g., whether a particular EU road freight measure drew on ITF sectoral work) is not established in the supplied source blocks and would require cross-referencing specific ITF publications against regulatory preambles.

**The brief does not resolve the operational status of the DTEE country outputs.** The DTEE project launch date of 22 May 2019 is documented, and the four participating countries are named, but the current completion status of individual country assessments for Argentina, Azerbaijan, India, and Morocco, and whether final mitigation action plans have been published, is not established from the supplied sources. *Specific publication dates and completion status of DTEE country reports not available from primary sources as of May 2026.*

**The brief does not resolve the Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative's work programme detail.** The successor initiative lists projects under development (East Africa Freight Transport, aligning transport and energy transition, trade in used vehicles), but the publication schedule, methodological outputs expected, and how those outputs will be made available to industry partners are not detailed in the supplied source blocks. *Specific work programme deliverables and publication timeline for the Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative not available from primary sources as of May 2026.*

**Does NOT resolve whether ITF modelling methodology meets the specific evidential standard required under CSRD or FuelEU reporting obligations — see legal review and EU Commission guidance for binding answer.**

---

**MONITORING — Re-check window: Q4 2026 (annual partner meeting cycle; next ITF Summit May 2027)**

The OECD International Transport Forum (ITF) Decarbonising Transport (DT) initiative is a multi-stakeholder, multi-year programme designed to supply governments and industry with evidence-based tools for selecting transport CO₂ mitigation measures. It is not a single research publication but a structured, ongoing initiative producing a rolling body of work across five work streams.

**Scale and emissions baseline.** Transport emits around 23% of the energy-related CO₂ that feeds global warming. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum (ITF/OECD), accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport.

Without immediate action, transport's share could reach 40% by 2030. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport.

Transport emissions have grown faster than those of any other sector over the past 50 years. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport.

Demand for transport will continue to grow massively in the coming decades, and CO₂ emissions from transport activity could increase by 60% by 2050 because transport relies on oil for 92% of its energy. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport.

**Divergence between OECD and non-OECD trajectories.** Transport accounted for 30% of CO₂ emissions in OECD countries in 2016; in non-OECD countries it contributed only 16%. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport in Emerging Economies (DTEE) project page, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://www.itf-oecd.org/dtee.

Transport emissions in OECD countries are expected to decrease by 1% annually through to 2030, according to ITF estimates; in non-OECD countries they will grow by 2%. *Source: ITF DTEE project page, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://www.itf-oecd.org/dtee.

Transport volumes in non-OECD countries are projected to grow more than twice as fast as in the OECD, with 4% annual growth for passenger and 5% for freight transport. *Source: ITF DTEE project page, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://www.itf-oecd.org/dtee.

**Five work streams.** The initiative is organised in five work streams: (1) tracking progress of current mitigation measures; (2) in-depth sectoral studies covering urban passenger transport, road freight transport, maritime transport, aviation, and inter-urban transport; (3) focus studies on specific decarbonisation issues; (4) national pathway assessments; and (5) policy dialogue through high-level roundtables, policy briefings, and technical workshops. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport.

**UNFCCC focal-point status.** The UN Climate Change Secretariat (UNFCCC) has named the International Transport Forum a focal point for transport under its Marrakech Partnership, in which role the ITF acts as a conduit for the exchange of information between the transport sector and the UNFCCC, as well as providing inputs to the UNFCCC process. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport.

**Governance and partner structure.** The initiative currently unites more than 70 governments, organisations, institutions, foundations and companies. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport. An annual meeting of project partners is held each May back-to-back with the Summit of transport ministers organised by the ITF, to discuss findings and review progress against the work plan. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative: Partners page, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://www.itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport-project-partners.

**Funding.** The initiative was launched in 2016 with core funding from the ITF's Corporate Partnership Board (CPB). Other funding partners currently include the governments of France, Korea, Ireland and the Netherlands, the World Bank, the European Commission, the Climate Works Foundation, the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the FIA Foundation, the International Road Transport Union (IRU), and the Swedish Shipowners' Association. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport.

**Key knowledge partners with direct freight relevance.** Among the listed knowledge partners, the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), Smart Freight Centre, Transport & Environment (T&E), the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the World Resources Institute (WRI) contribute to the initiative; the European Association for Forwarding, Transport, Logistics and Customs Services (CLECAT) and the International Federation of Freight Forwarders Associations (FIATA) participate as professional and sectoral associations. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative: Partners page, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://www.itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport-project-partners.

**Emerging-economy sub-project (DTEE).** The Decarbonising Transport in Emerging Economies (DTEE) project supports transport decarbonisation in Argentina, Azerbaijan, India, and Morocco. It is designing a common assessment framework for transport emissions that will cover several transport sub-sectors and transport modes. The project is carried out in collaboration with the Wuppertal Institute (WI) and is supported by the International Climate Initiative (IKI) of the German Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety (BMWK). *Source: ITF DTEE project page, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://www.itf-oecd.org/dtee.

**Evolution to Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative.** The DT initiative has evolved into a broader initiative focused on implementing sustainable transport policies — the Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative, launched during the ITF 2024 Summit. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport. The Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative is described explicitly as an evolution of ITF's Decarbonising Transport initiative. *Source: ITF Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative page, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://www.itf-oecd.org/sustainable-transport-systems-initiative.

**Methodology.** The assessments of the Decarbonising Transport initiative are grounded in data analysis and advanced modelling; uniquely, the ITF modelling framework derives projections of transport activity from analysing the drivers of demand and then models how changes in mobility patterns affect CO₂ emissions. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport. The successor Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative uses the ITF's PASTA framework, which includes indicators to assess welfare and SDGs such as local pollutants, safety, congestion, vehicle space consumption, accessibility, affordability, and resilience. *Source: ITF Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative page, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://www.itf-oecd.org/sustainable-transport-systems-initiative.

**Scope limitation of this brief.** The source blocks provided are the initiative's programme-level web pages and the DTEE and Sustainable Transport Systems sub-project pages. They describe the initiative's design, governance, participants, and headline findings, but the full corpus of sector-specific analytical outputs (individual road freight studies, maritime decarbonisation reports, aviation sector analyses, and country pathway assessments) is not contained in the supplied source blocks. Those outputs are flagged in the New Sources Identified section for retrieval.

---

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- "The ITF's Decarbonising Transport initiative, which unites more than 70 governments and organisations including FIATA and CLECAT, projects that transport CO₂ emissions could increase by 60% by 2050 without intervention, and that transport's current 23% share of energy-related CO₂ could reach 40% by 2030." This is a FACT directly from a primary intergovernmental source and is citable by name without qualification.
- "The ITF has formal UNFCCC focal-point status for transport, meaning its analytical outputs feed directly into climate negotiation processes — not just academic debate." This positions ITF findings as policy-relevant, not merely academic.
- "Freight transport in non-OECD markets is projected to grow at 5% annually, against a 1% annual decrease in OECD transport emissions — which means the compliance burden on our clients' supply chains through emerging-market corridors is structurally increasing, not decreasing, over the medium term."
- "FIATA and CLECAT both participate in the ITF initiative, so the guidance those associations publish on freight decarbonisation is methodologically anchored to the same ITF evidence base."

**Questions to pose to clients:**

- "Has your Scope 3 calculation methodology been aligned with the ITF/GLEC/ISO 14083 approach? That alignment is increasingly what auditors and regulators are asking for."
- "Which of your trade lanes run through non-OECD corridors where low-carbon freight capacity is currently limited? That's where the greatest emissions exposure is building fastest."
- "When you set a net-zero target date, have you modelled the 60% emissions growth baseline scenario, or assumed a flat baseline?"

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

- Do not claim that the ITF "recommends" or "endorses" any specific fuel, modal choice, or service the workspace offers. The initiative explicitly does not advocate specific measures. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport. Clients or auditors who check this will find the caveat, and an overclaim damages credibility.
- Do not conflate the DT initiative with the successor Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative when citing specific publications. Check publication dates and the initiative under which they were produced.
- Do not present ITF projections (23%, 40%, 60%, 5%) as regulatory thresholds or compliance obligations. They are analytical projections, not binding targets.
- *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any ITF-derived methodology (e.g. as adopted by Smart Freight Centre's GLEC Framework or ISO 14083) constitutes a binding reporting standard under a specific regulation that applies to the workspace — such as EU CSRD or FuelEU — requires legal and compliance review against the specific regulation's text.

---

**The 23%-to-40% trajectory is the baseline for regulatory pressure across all modes the workspace uses.**

*Operational implication:* The ITF's finding that transport's share of energy-related CO₂ emissions could rise from 23% to 40% by 2030 without immediate action is the analytical foundation that regulators cite when designing mandatory measures — including the EU's FuelEU Maritime regulation, ICAO's CORSIA scheme, the EU ETS extension to aviation and shipping, and national road freight CO₂ standards. For workspaces operating across air, road, and ocean modes, this trajectory is not background context; it is the driver behind the compliance cost pipeline.

*Operational implication:* The ITF's 5% annual freight volume growth projection for non-OECD countries is directly relevant to workspaces with trade lanes running into or through emerging markets in Asia, Latin America, the Middle East, and Africa. That growth rate, compounded against low current decarbonisation investment in those corridors, signals that lane-level emissions intensity will increase before it decreases, raising Scope 3 reporting obligations for the workspace and its clients in those corridors before compliant capacity arrives.

**FIATA and CLECAT participation converts ITF output into industry-facing guidance.**

*Operational implication:* FIATA and CLECAT both participate in the Decarbonising Transport initiative as professional and sectoral associations. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative: Partners page, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://www.itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport-project-partners. Analytical inference: ITF findings on road freight and aviation decarbonisation pathways are therefore likely to be referenced in FIATA and CLECAT guidance documents that the workspace's compliance function would ordinarily track. This makes the ITF corpus a primary source, not merely academic context.

**The shift to the Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative signals a move from analysis to implementation.**

*Analytical inference:* The explicit framing of the Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative as an evolution that focuses on implementing sustainable transport policies, and its four-step model that ends in "dialogues identify actions and support implementation," indicates that ITF output is moving from describing options to actively driving policy adoption. For the workspace, this means ITF publications will increasingly carry implementation timetables and policy levers — material that directly affects the compliance calendar.

**The 92% oil dependency figure quantifies the structural lock-in that makes rapid decarbonisation of air and road freight expensive.**

*Analytical inference:* The ITF's finding that transport relies on oil for 92% of its energy, combined with a 60% emissions growth projection to 2050, is the quantitative underpinning for both the urgency and the cost of mandatory fuel switching. For workspaces with air as the primary mode and road as secondary, this lock-in figure explains why SAF mandates and road fleet CO₂ standards impose above-inflation cost trajectories: the alternatives are not yet at scale or price parity.

**Emerging-economy freight growth (5% per year) is the most operationally relevant ITF statistic for corridor planning.**

*Operational implication:* For the workspace's trade lanes involving non-OECD markets — including Asia-Pacific and Latin American corridors — the ITF DTEE finding that freight transport volumes in non-OECD countries grow at 5% annually, while emissions reduction policy in those countries lags OECD markets, creates a structural gap between growing lane demand and compliant capacity. Workspaces that commit early to carriers or routes with credible low-carbon capacity in those corridors gain both Scope 3 advantage and supply security ahead of regulatory tightening.

---

**1. Scope 3 emissions disclosures — quantitative basis for carrier selection criteria**

*Analytical inference:* The ITF's modelling framework, which derives CO₂ projections from transport demand drivers, is the same methodological lineage underpinning ISO 14083 (transport emissions calculation) and GLEC Framework guidance from Smart Freight Centre — both of which FIATA has recommended as reporting standards. The workspace can anchor its carrier selection criteria in ITF-consistent methodology, strengthening the defensibility of Scope 3 calculations under CSRD and voluntary client disclosures. This is a specific decision: when evaluating carrier bids, the workspace should ask whether carrier-supplied emissions data aligns with the ITF modelling approach or a recognised derivative (ISO 14083, GLEC).

**2. Client sustainability commitments — avoid overstating ITF authority**

*Analytical inference:* The ITF initiative does not advocate specific measures or policies; it identifies options for decision-makers. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative overview, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport. This is a material constraint on how the workspace can cite ITF findings in client proposals. The workspace can accurately state that ITF analysis identifies road freight decarbonisation as a priority work stream with sectoral pathway studies underway; it cannot state that ITF has endorsed a specific modal shift, fuel type, or service offering.

**3. Emerging-market routing decisions — the DTEE gap is now on record**

*Analytical inference:* The DTEE project covers Argentina, Azerbaijan, India, and Morocco. The workspace's trade lanes into Asia-Pacific beyond India, into sub-Saharan Africa, and into Southeast Asia fall outside the current DTEE country scope. This is a documented gap: ITF sectoral analysis for those corridors is either covered by the broader DT initiative or not yet published. Routing decisions for those lanes cannot currently be supported by ITF country-pathway modelling equivalent to what is available for OECD markets, and the workspace should note this when constructing sustainability claims about those routes.

**4. The 2024 evolution to Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative — update internal reference documents**

*Analytical inference:* References to "the ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative" in the workspace's internal compliance documents, client-facing sustainability reports, or RFP responses should now note that the initiative has formally evolved into the Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative. Citing the DT initiative without noting its evolution may cause confusion in client or auditor review, particularly where the workspace references the initiative as evidence of regulatory alignment.

**5. Annual partner meeting cadence sets the workspace's monitoring trigger**

*Analytical inference:* The annual partner meeting held each May back-to-back with the ITF Summit is the mechanism through which updated findings and work-plan progress are reviewed. *Source: ITF Decarbonising Transport initiative: Partners page, International Transport Forum, accessed May 2026. https://www.itf-oecd.org/decarbonising-transport-project-partners. The workspace should schedule a review of ITF publications each June (after the May Summit cycle) to capture new sectoral guidance before it is absorbed into client sustainability expectations or regulatory proposals.

Active Projects Policy Dialogue Partners Sign-up for the Decarbonising Transport Newsletter Video of Reshaping transport for a cleaner environment and fairer society The Decarbonising Transport initiative promotes carbon-neutral mobility to help stop climate change. It provides decision makers with tools to select CO 2 mitigation measures that deliver on their climate commitment. Climate change affects lives around the globe. Rising temperatures cause droughts, rising sea levels threaten low-lying regions, ever more extreme weather leads to severe disruptions. Climate change cannot be stopped without decarbonising transport. Transport emits around 23% of the energy-related CO 2 that feeds global warming. Without imm ediate action, its share could reach 40% by 2030. Transport emissions have grown faster than those of any other sector over the past 50 years.  Demand for transport will continue to grow massively in the coming decades. As a result CO 2 emissions from transport activity will not fall, but could increase by 60% by 2050. And because transport relies on oil for 92% of its energy, it is particularly hard to decarbonise .  The Decarbonising Transport initiative helps  governments and industry to translate climate ambitions into actions. Specifically, it: Builds a catalogue of effective CO 2 mitigation measures: the Transport Climate Action Directory . Provides  targeted analytical assistance for countries and partners to identify climate actions that work. Gathers and shares evidence for best practices that will accelerate the transition to carbon-neutral mobility. Shapes the climate change debate by building a global policy dialogue and by bringing the transport perspective to the broader climate change discussions.  The Decarbonising Transport initiative is organised in five work streams: Tracking progress: The initiative evaluates how current mitigation measures contribute to reaching objectives for reducing transport CO 2 . In-depth sectoral studies: The initiative identifies effective policies for decarbonising urban passenger transport, road freight transport, maritime transport, aviation and inter-urban transport. Focus studies: The initiative analyses specific decarbonisation issues and feeds the results into other work streams. National pathways: The initiative assesses available policy levers for decarbonising transport from a country perspective. Projects may also examine regional or sub-national levels. Policy Dialogue: The initiative organises global dialogue on transport and climate change through high-level roundtables, policy briefings and technical workshops. It acts as a conduit for transport sector input to climate change negotiations. The Decarbonising Transport initiative does not advocate specific measures or policies. Building on an evidence-based assessment of mitigation impacts, it identifies options for decision-makers to achieve their targets -  for   instance   the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) submitted by countries under the Paris Agreement, as well as targets set by sectors, companies or cities.    The assessments of the Decarbonising Transport initiative are grounded in data analysis and advanced modelling . Uniquely, the ITF modelling framework derives projections of transport activity from analysing the drivers of demand. It then models how changes in mobility patterns affect CO 2 emissions. All work streams of the Decarbonising Transport initiative are open for involvement. The initiative currently unites more than 70 governments, organisations , institutions, foundations and companies. Partners contribute in different roles including as funders and knowledge partners. The Decarbonising Transport initiative was launched in 2016 with core funding from the ITF’s Corporate Partnership Board (CPB). Other funding partners currently include the governments of France, Korea, Ireland and the Netherlands, the World Bank, the European Commission, the Climate Works Foundation, the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the FIA Foundation, the International Road Transport Union (IRU) and the Swedish Shipowners' Association. In recognition of the work of its Decarbonising Transport initiative, the UN Climate Change Secretariat (UNFCCC) has named the International Transport Forum a focal point for transport under its Marrakech Partnership. In this role, the ITF acts as a conduit for the exchange of information between the transport sector and the UNFCCC, as well as providing inputs to the UNFCCC process. The DT initiative has evolved into a broader initiative focused on implementing sustainable transport policies. Azerbaijan India Morocco DTEE Events Sign-up for the Decarbonising Transport Newsletter One of the biggest challenges for climate change mitigation is to enable emerging economies to continue lifting people out of poverty while at the same time reducing greenhouse gas emissions. The ITF’s Decarbonising Transport in Emerging Economies (DTEE) project helps governments of emerging nations to identify ways to reduce their transport CO 2 emissions and meet their climate goals. The DTEE project supports transport decarbonisation in Argentina, Azerbaijan, India and Morocco. It is designing a common assessment framework for transport emissions that will cover several transport sub-sectors and transport modes. Country-specific modelling tools and policy scenarios will help the participating governments to implement ambitious CO 2 -reduction initiatives for their transport sectors. Stakeholder workshops, training sessions, briefings for policy makers and mitigation action plans will stimulate further research and the development of policies beyond the duration of the project. Transport is a major enabler of economic development. But it is also a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions. Transport accounted for 30% of CO 2 emissions in OECD countries in 2016. In non-OECD countries it contributed only 16%. But transport emissions in the OECD are expected to decrease by 1% annually through to 2030, according to ITF estimates. In non-OECD countries they will grow by 2%. This is mostly because transport demand there grows significantly faster. Estimates see transport volumes in non-OECD countries grow more than twice as fast as in the OECD with 4% annual growth for passenger and 5% for freight transport. Transport CO 2 emissions per capita in emerging economies are still well below the OECD average. In India, the CO 2 emitted per inhabitant was almost one-twentieth that of an average OECD country. Thus, an average person in India contributes less CO 2 in a year than someone taking one transatlantic roundtrip flight. Emerging economies can hardly be expected to curb their economic development and stop improving living standards as the price for limiting climate change. The challenge is therefore to accommodate the growing transport demand that often comes with economic development in an environmentally sustainable way. To tackle this challenge, the International Transport Forum, in collaboration with the Wuppertal Institute (WI) and supported by the International Climate Initiative (IKI) of the German Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety (BMWK), is carrying out the Decarbonising Transport in Emerging Economies (DTEE) project. In the context of the ITF’s wider Decarbonising Transport (DT) initiative, the DTEE project will help governments of emerging countries to establish pathways to reducing transport CO 2 emissions and meet CO 2 reduction pledges under the Paris Agreement. The participating countries are Argentina; Azerbaijan; India, and Morocco. For them, the ITF will design a tailor-made transport emissions assessment framework. This will account for all the countries’ relevant characteristics including their development plans, and enable governments to better understand current and future transport activity and related CO 2 emissions. Modelling tools and policy scenarios will help to identify effective transport CO 2 mitigation measures. The project team works in close cooperation and coordination with the participating countries’ government agencies, local decision-makers, researchers, other experts and civil society organisations. Stakeholder workshops, training events and the dissemination of project findings will help build capacity for future transport research and policy development well beyond the duration of the project. The four participating countries represent a wide range of challenges for the decarbonisaton of transport in emerging economies. They differ with regard to world region, economic specificities and infrastructure characteristics. They share similarities in that all four have lower transport CO 2 emissions per capita than the OECD average, but higher growth rates of transport activity. In all of them, meeting increasing transport demand while reducing CO 2 emissions is a critical challenge for policy makers. Governing Resilient Transport 12 - 14 May 2027 Leipzig, Germany, International Transport Forum See all events > Toggle navigation Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative This initiative promotes sustainable transport, helping to achieve the UN Sustainable Development Goals. It identifies the challenges governments face in developing sustainable transport policies and supports policy makers to implement solutions. Prosperity requires access to opportunities. Alongside proximity and virtual connectivity, transport connects people with opportunities. But transport uses finite resources, like energy and space, and exacerbates the climate emergency through greenhouse gas emissions and local pollutants. Transport is relevant to achieving each of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) as it provides vital access to opportunities. To meet current needs without comprising the future, transport policies must be consistent with health, environmental, and decarbonisation objectives, and use resources sustainably. This is the principle of Sustainable Transport. The Sustainable Transport Systems Initiative engages and mobilises stakeholders. Using systemic analysis based on ITF's world-class models, it identifies options to overcome challenges to achieving sustainable transport. The project supports dialogue between actors in the system to offer implementable solutions for policy makers. It is an example of collective problem-solving.  Each project within this initiative follows a four-step process: Step 1. Identify specific challenges countries are facing Engaging with ITF’s Transport Research Committee, surveying ITF's member countries, and building on previous ITF work. These challenges may be globally relevant or specific to a region. Step 2. Propose options by mapping systemic relationships between different sectors ITF’s world-leading PASTA framework includes indicators to assess welfare and SDGs. Indicators related to SDGs include local pollutants, safety, congestion, vehicle space consumption, accessibility, affordability and resilience. The project also works to expand ITF models to include indicators that relate to more SDGs and welfare assessment enabled by transport. This phase exposes the interactions, independencies, and tensions between different policy areas to achieve common goals. Step 3: Mobilise the system of actors across government, industry and NGOs Sustainability challenges cannot be resolved by the transport sector alone. It requires action and alignment from policy makers from transport and non-transport actors. Step 4: Dialogues identify actions and support implementation  for each challenge Transport and non-transport sectors are mobilised through ITF's strategic relationships, bringing them together in dialogue focused on implementation. Projects already under development include: East Africa Freight Transport: Building Regional Connectivity Defining accessibility goals Aligning the transport and energy transition Understanding the
